facts.text: Tardigrades (water bears) can survive being cooled to -272°C (just one degree above absolute zero) and heated to 150°C, withstand pressures six times greater than the deepest ocean trenches, and have survived direct exposure to the vacuum of space for at least 10 days—yet they die if their habitat simply dries out too quickly without entering their protective tun state first.
facts.verification_note: Scientific studies confirm tardigrades can survive these extreme conditions when in their desiccated "tun" state, but rapid desiccation that prevents proper tun formation is indeed lethal to them.
facts.image_description: The illustration should depict a split-scene composition in a detailed scientific-meets-surreal style: on the left, a magnified tardigrade floats triumphantly in the harsh void of space, surrounded by swirling cosmic nebulae in deep purples and blues, with ice crystals forming on its translucent body and pressure waves radiating around it in glowing orange and white to represent extreme conditions. On the right side, contrasting sharply, the same tardigrade lies vulnerable and withering on cracked, sun-bleached earth rendered in harsh yellows and browns, its eight legs curled inward, with a single drop of water evaporating into steam nearby—a beam of golden sunlight piercing through creates dramatic lighting that emphasizes the irony of its weakness. The tardigrade itself should be rendered in translucent, jewel-like detail showing its segmented body and clawed feet, with a slight anthropomorphic quality to its "face" that conveys both resilience and fragility. facts.text: Mantis shrimp can punch with an acceleration of over 10,000 times the force of gravity, creating cavitation bubbles that collapse with a flash of light reaching temperatures around 4,700°C—nearly as hot as the surface of the sun.
facts.verification_note: Mantis shrimp strikes do reach accelerations over 10,000 g, produce cavitation bubbles that emit sonoluminescence at temperatures around 4,700°C, which is comparable to the sun's surface temperature of approximately 5,500°C.
facts.image_description: A split-second photorealistic capture shows a vibrant peacock mantis shrimp—its body displaying electric blues, greens, and oranges—mid-strike in crystalline ocean water. Its raptorial appendage blurs forward in a motion streak, surrounded by a constellation of translucent cavitation bubbles that glow from within with brilliant white-yellow light, like miniature stars igniting. The focal bubble at impact point erupts in an intense plasma-like flash of orange and white (4,700°C), creating a small shockwave ring visible in the disturbed water, while a small thermometer graphic or temperature overlay in the corner compares this heat to the sun's surface. The composition uses dramatic side-lighting to emphasize the explosive energy, with the darker blue ocean background making the bioluminescent-like flashes pop, and motion lines or speed indicators subtly integrated to convey the 10,000g acceleration force.

facts.text: The platypus is one of the few venomous mammals, with males possessing ankle spurs that deliver venom powerful enough to cause severe pain in humans that cannot be relieved by morphine and can last for weeks. The venom contains defensin-like proteins that are unique to monotremes and cause rapid swelling and muscle wasting around the affected area.
facts.verification_note: All stated facts are scientifically accurate: male platypuses have venomous ankle spurs, the venom causes severe morphine-resistant pain lasting weeks, and contains defensin-like proteins (DLPs) unique to monotremes that cause swelling and muscle wasting.
facts.image_description: A detailed scientific cross-section illustration showing a male platypus's hind leg in the foreground, with the distinctive ankle spur prominently displayed in burnished ivory and amber tones, droplets of translucent venom glistening at its tip. The composition splits into two panels: the left showing the spur's internal anatomy with the venom gland rendered in deep purples and reds, connected by delicate ducts illustrated in medical textbook style; the right panel depicting a ghostly, semi-transparent human hand in pale blues and grays with areas of angry red inflammation and swelling, overlaid with molecular diagrams of the unique defensin-like proteins floating like luminescent geometric structures. The background features a muted teal gradient with subtle anatomical sketches of the full platypus, while clinical labels and arrows in crisp white text connect each element, creating a bridge between natural history illustration and modern medical imaging with dramatic side-lighting that emphasizes the spur's dangerous elegance.
